title: Install Ubuntu 22.04 on VM 106 unattended (cloud image + cloud-init)
description:
VM 106 (palworld-server) has NO operating system: its only disk, local-lvm:vm-106-disk-0 (100G), has never been written (`lvs` Data% 0.00, no partition table — the engine measured this on 2026-10-02; ADD5's install was removed by ADD53's `pvesm free`). Install Ubuntu Server 22.04 on VM 106 UNATTENDED — no console interaction at any point — the Proxmox way, from the host (the runner runs here as root):

1. Download the Ubuntu 22.04 (jammy) cloud image to the host if it is not already there: `curl -fL -o /var/lib/vz/template/jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.img https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/jammy/current/jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.img` (about 700 MB).
2. Stop VM 106 if it is running (`qm status 106 | grep -q running && qm stop 106`), then import the image as a new disk on local-lvm (`qm importdisk 106 /var/lib/vz/template/jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.img local-lvm` — it appears as `unused0`, named vm-106-disk-1), attach it as the boot disk (`qm set 106 --scsihw virtio-scsi-pci --scsi0 local-lvm:vm-106-disk-1 --boot order=scsi0`) and grow it to 100G (`qm resize 106 scsi0 100G`; cloud-init grows the filesystem on first boot). The old empty disk vm-106-disk-0 becomes unused: detach and free it (`qm set 106 --delete unused0` after confirming which unusedN it is, then `pvesm free local-lvm:vm-106-disk-0`) — nothing is lost, it was never written.
3. Attach a cloud-init drive and seed it: `qm set 106 --ide2 local-lvm:cloudinit --ciuser aedefruscio --cipassword "$MASS_PASSWORD" --sshkeys /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub --ipconfig0 ip=dhcp --nameserver 192.168.1.1 --agent 1 --serial0 socket --vga serial0`. The password is the stored MASS_PASSWORD, referenced BY NAME exactly as written (the runner expands it; the value never appears in any block); the SSH key is this host's own public key, so the engine can log in afterwards.
4. Start VM 106 (`qm start 106`), then wait for it to come up on the network: its NIC MAC is in `qm config 106` (net0); loop up to 12 × 10 s over a sweep (`nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 >/dev/null 2>&1`) and `ip neigh show | grep -i <mac>` until an address appears, then `ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new aedefruscio@<address> 'lsb_release -ds'` until it answers (cloud-init needs a minute on first boot).

Done when that ssh prints "Ubuntu 22.04…" and `qm config 106` shows scsi0 = local-lvm:vm-106-disk-1 (100G) and ide2 = the cloud-init drive. Installing qemu-guest-agent inside the guest is ADD82's job, not this step's. The whole sequence is one bash script under ## Write these files, run as `MASS_PASSWORD="$MASS_PASSWORD" bash /tmp/<name>.sh`; every lookup a wait loop expects to be empty ends in `|| true`.

title: Reset VM 106 and capture its serial console during boot (why it has no address)
description: VM 106 (palworld-server) boots Ubuntu from its new cloud-image disk and talks on the wire (the bridge learned its MAC), yet it has no network address under either a DHCP seed or the static seed ipconfig0 ip=192.168.1.106/24,gw=192.168.1.1 — and a newline sent to its serial console (ADD118) produced nothing in six seconds: the guest is not interactive on its console. The boot log is the witness that remains. From the host: capture the serial console (serial0: socket, /var/run/qemu-server/106.serial0) for about 140 seconds while the VM is hard-reset (qm reset 106 — it has no state worth keeping until it reaches the network), then print the tail: GRUB, the kernel command line, systemd's network targets, cloud-init's datasource line (NoCloud or "no datasource"), its ci-info network table, and the login prompt. That text decides the fix to the install step.

title: LXC 111: implement the Palworld settings capability (read/write the server's own settings file)
description:
On LXC 111, add a backend route that reads and writes the Palworld server's settings (switches etc.) by editing the Palworld config file at PALWORLD_IP 192.168.1.106 over SSH as PALWORLD_USER aedefruscio, exposing GET/PUT of the settings keys. No UI yet. On container 111.

[Engine split of ADD100 — 2 of 8] Done when the capability WORKS, not when its code exists (operator decision 2026-10-07): `pct exec 111 -- curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/palworld-settings` returns the server's real settings including `ServerName` (from the live /opt/palworld/Pal/Saved/Config/LinuxServer/PalWorldSettings.ini, or from /opt/palworld/DefaultPalWorldSettings.ini while the live file is empty). The SAVE path is proven before delivery by the engine's rehearsal (a GET-then-PUT round trip on copies of the real files from VM 106 that must leave every setting and the header intact), so verifying it on the live machine -- which would stop and start the game server -- is not part of this step; the first real save is the operator's, from the panel. (The path follows the capability registry that ADD121 built: /opt/control-panel-backend/config/capabilities.json gives this capability the id `palworld-settings`.)

title: LXC 111: implement the media request capability (Radarr/Sonarr request path)
description:
On LXC 111, add a backend route that takes a movie/TV title and calls the Radarr (192.168.1.22:7878) and Sonarr lookup/add APIs to make the media server fetch it, using API keys read from a config file the operator's values populate. No UI yet. On container 111.

[Engine split of ADD100 — 3 of 8] Done when the capability WORKS, not when its code exists (operator decision 2026-10-07): `pct exec 111 -- curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Sintel","type":"movie"}' http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/media-request` answers 200 with Radarr's entry for Sintel. A title already in the library is a request already satisfied: the route answers 200 with that library entry and `"alreadyInLibrary": true`, and asks Radarr to add nothing -- Sintel IS in the library (ADD134 added it), so this check changes nothing in Radarr. A missing key, a 401, a connection error or any non-200 answer is a failure. (The path follows the capability registry that ADD121 built: config/capabilities.json gives this capability the id `media-request`.)

title: LXC 111: implement the scaffold-engine capability (reach the engine's own AI surface)

No UI yet. On container 111.

[Engine split of ADD100 — 4 of 8] Done when the capability WORKS, not when its code exists (operator decision 2026-10-07): the panel's route for the registry's `scaffold-engine` capability, `/api/scaffold-engine` (the registry's id, as `/api/palworld-settings` and `/api/media-request` are), returns scaffold-engine's own /health answer: `pct exec 111 -- curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/scaffold-engine` answers JSON with `"status":"healthy"` -- not a connection error.

title: LXC 111: implement the network-view capability (read-only Pi-hole API)
description:
On LXC 111, add a backend route that reads Pi-hole's own API (LXC 130) for queries, block fraction, top blocked domains, and per-client activity, read-only, with the Pi-hole address read from config. (Measured 2026-10-08: this is Pi-hole v6.4.3 with NO password set, so its v6 API -- `/api/stats/summary` -- answers without any token; there is no token to configure.) No UI yet. On container 111.

[Engine split of ADD100 — 5 of 8] Done when the capability WORKS, not when its code exists (operator decision 2026-10-07): the panel's route for the `network-view` capability, `/api/network-view` (registered in config/capabilities.json beside the others), returns Pi-hole's own summary: `pct exec 111 -- curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/network-view` answers JSON with a numeric count of DNS queries and of blocked queries -- not an auth or connection error. Read-only: it changes nothing in Pi-hole.

title: LXC 111: add authentication and wire the systemd service so the panel runs and survives reboot
description:
On LXC 111, add a single authentication layer (password/token from config) in front of the whole panel, create the control-panel.service systemd unit, enable and start it, and confirm it listens on the container's address. On container 111.

[Engine split of ADD100 — 7 of 8] Done when the gate WORKS (operator decisions 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-08): every route and page of the panel asks for HTTP Basic credentials -- user `panel`, password the runner's secret `PANEL_PASSWORD` (the operator stores it in Settings -> Machines; the engine never sees it). Without credentials `pct exec 111 -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w %{http_code} http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/palworld-settings` answers `401`; with them `pct exec 111 -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w %{http_code} -u panel:"$PANEL_PASSWORD" http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/palworld-settings` answers `200`; and `pct exec 111 -- systemctl is-enabled control-panel.service` answers `enabled`.

title: Give the control panel an ssh key it can use on VM 106 (palworld-server)
description:
The panel's Palworld page reads and writes the game server's own settings file over ssh, from container 111 to VM 106, every time the operator opens it. Nothing has given that service a credential there, so without this step the page fails with publickey the first time it is used while the step that wrote it still reports success.

MEASURED 2026-10-04: `control-panel.service` in CT 111 declares no `User=`, so the panel runs as root and /root/.ssh already exists there. VM 106 is at 192.168.1.106, its agent answers, and `/home/aedefruscio/.ssh/authorized_keys` holds 2 keys.

DO NOT ask anyone to paste the key, and do not use this host's own key: the key that must be installed is the one belonging to the PANEL, inside container 111. The two machines are reached from the Proxmox host, so write ONE host-side script and run it, capturing the key in a variable so no value is ever pasted:
```
pct exec 111 -- sh -c 'test -f /root/.ssh/id_ed25519 || ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f /root/.ssh/id_ed25519'
KEY="$(pct exec 111 -- cat /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub)"
[ -n "$KEY" ] || { echo 'FAILED: no public key in 111'; exit 1; }
qm guest exec 106 -- sh -c "cp -a /home/aedefruscio/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/aedefruscio/.ssh/authorized_keys.bak.\$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S); printf '%s\\n' '$KEY' >> /home/aedefruscio/.ssh/authorized_keys"
```
Append, never overwrite: two keys are already there and both are in use.

Done when `qm guest exec 106 -- sh -c 'wc -l < /home/aedefruscio/.ssh/authorized_keys'` reads 3 and `pct exec 111 -- ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new aedefruscio@192.168.1.106 true` succeeds from inside the container.

title: Proxmox firewall: enforce the security groups on every guest
description:
Operator decision 2026-10-10: turn on the Proxmox firewall for each guest using the security groups in /etc/pve/firewall/cluster.fw. The exact content of every file is below — write it LITERALLY (these were written from the ports each guest measurably listens on, 2026-10-10/11). All files are on the Proxmox HOST (/etc/pve is the host's); write them from the runner's own shell, never through pct exec / qm guest exec. Do NOT change host.fw.

Rule order matters: each group in cluster.fw ends with `IN DROP`, and a group's rules apply where its GROUP line sits, so every guest's own rules come BEFORE its GROUP line.

1–2. ALREADY DONE (2026-10-11 02:03 UTC, verified): /etc/pve/firewall/cluster.fw is backed up to /etc/pve/firewall/cluster.fw.bak.add151 and its `[group dmz]` section already reads the four lines this step wants. Do NOT touch cluster.fw or its backup again — re-running the backup would overwrite the original with the edited file.
3. Write each guest's file with exactly this content. The runner's shell is unprivileged and sudo elevates only the command, so a `cat > FILE` / `> FILE` redirect is refused (Permission denied, live): write each file as `printf '%s\n' '<line 1>' '<line 2>' … | tee /etc/pve/firewall/<id>.fw` (tee runs as root).

   /etc/pve/firewall/101.fw:

    enable: 1
    policy_in: DROP
    
    [RULES]
    IN ACCEPT -p tcp -dport 22 -source 192.168.1.0/24

title: Install and enable QEMU Guest Agent in VM 106
description:
Install qemu-guest-agent inside the palworld-server guest (VM 106) and confirm it answers.

MEASURED ON THE HOST (read-only, just checked):
  qm status 106      -> running, booting from scsi0 (100G)
  qm agent 106 ping  -> "QEMU guest agent is not running"
  ip neigh           -> no entry for the VM's NIC bc:24:11:e8:9f:7a
  qm config 106      -> agent: 1 is ALREADY set on the VM

The host therefore has NO way in to this guest right now, and three methods are
ruled out by that, not by preference:
  - `pct exec 106` cannot address a VM at all (pct is for containers).
  - `qm guest exec 106` needs the agent that this step installs. Chicken and egg.
  - SSH needs an address, and the guest has no network presence the host can see.

So this one is done at the console, by hand:
  1. Open https://192.168.1.156:8006, select VM 106 (palworld-server), click Console.
  2. Log in to the guest.
  3. Install and start the agent:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-guest-agent
sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
systemctl is-active qemu-guest-agent
```

  4. If the guest has no network either, fix that first — apt cannot reach the
     mirrors without it — and say so here rather than working around it.

`agent: 1` is already set on the VM, so nothing is needed on the host side.
Done when `qm agent 106 ping` answers from the host (that is ADD65).

ENGINE CORRECTION (2026-10-02): the lines above that say "NO way in to this guest right now, and three methods are"; "Chicken and egg"; "no network presence the host can see"; "done at the console, by hand:" are SUPERSEDED -- the engine measured otherwise after they were written: `sudo apt-get update` runs in the runner's own shell on the Proxmox HOST, and the step is about VM/CT 106 -- live, this would have installed qemu-guest-agent on the host instead of in VM 106 (a `qm agent 106 ping` beside it is a read and reaches nothing). Every command that CHANGES something must reach the guest: a container with `pct exec 106 -- <command>`; a VM with `qm guest exec 106 -- <command>` (needs the agent) or over ssh -- and a VM WITHOUT the agent is reached by finding its address from its MAC (`qm config 106` → net0 MAC → `ip neigh show`, after `qm start 106` and a wait) and `SSHPASS="$MASS_PASSWORD" sshpass -e ssh-copy-id -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new <user>@<address>`, as ONE bash script under ## Write these files run with `MASS_PASSWORD="$MASS_PASSWORD" bash /tmp/<name>.sh`. A host-side operation ON the guest is `qm …/pct … 106`. The step is the operator's only when ssh itself is refused -- say which command refused and why. The commands quoted above are the GUEST's and run inside it through that ssh. The account inside guest 106 is <PALWORLD_USER> (the operator fills it; nothing the engine holds names it); the password is `$MASS_PASSWORD`, by name. Nothing here is done at a console by hand.
